title: Balanga Secures First International Sales for History Doc ‘Beasts of the Colosseum,’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous (EXCLUSIVE)
description: International distributor Balanga has announced its first major international sales of its documentary “Beasts of the Colosseum,” produced by Antoin
body:
International distributor Balanga has announced its first major international sales of its documentary “Beasts of the Colosseum,” produced by Antoine Henriquet’s AH! Production and Jean-Luc Berlot’s Adline for Novo 19 in France, in association with Mediaset in Italy.

	ZDF/Terra X in Germany, SVT in Sweden and Radio-Canada have acquired the history documentary, which tells the story of the Venationes in Ancient Rome, extraordinary battles that featured exotic wild beasts instead of gladiators. Using extensive historical research and AI-driven reenactments, the doc describes the intricate system created to capture and transport thousands of animals from across the Roman Empire to fight in the Colosseum games.
	



	

									Christophe Bochnacki, President of Balanga
	



	“I believe we are entering a new generation of history documentaries. AI gives us the ability to bring stories, places and historical worlds to the screen that were previously beyond the economics of documentary production. For international audiences, that creates a new level of immersion and visual ambition,” said Christophe Bochnacki, President of Balanga.


	“The film explores the moment when nature stopped being simply observed or studied, and began to be staged, dramatized and consumed as entertainment,” Bochnacki added.

	The doc world premiered out of competition at the Cannes AI Film Festival, and will have its first screening for international buyers at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre on September 8.



	

									Producer Enora Contant, ‘Beasts of the Colosseum’
	



	Variety had a chance to interview the doc’s producer, Enora Contant, ahead of its screening at Unifrance Rendez-Vous.
	

	Why did you decide to make a documentary about the Venationes?

	Enora Contant: Like many viewers, I was deeply struck by the tiger scene in Ridley Scott’s “Gladiator.” It brought back those stories we first encounter at school – of men being thrown to wild beasts in Roman arenas – which fascinate us as much as they terrify us. And yet, one question is rarely asked: Where did all these animals come from? We know a great deal about the fate of the men who took part in the Roman games, but far less about the animals themselves.

	Why do you think there was such a fascination with the Venationes in ancient Rome?

	Contant: The games were at the heart of Roman social and political life. They offered an extraordinary collective spectacle, but they were also a demonstration of power. Bringing lions, elephants, bears or crocodiles to Rome from the furthest reaches of the Empire was a way of displaying the extent of the world Rome had conquered. As Katia Schörle, one of the experts featured in the film, explains, wild animals embodied a world that was both magnificent and terrifying. By exhibiting and then dominating them in the arena, Rome was symbolically asserting its mastery over nature itself.

	Can you elaborate on how you used AI in the documentary?

	Contant: We used AI to create all the historical reenactments: the capture expeditions, the transportation of the animals, the backstage areas of the Colosseum and the spectacles inside the arena. Every sequence is developed from rigorous historical research. The settings, costumes, animals, props and gestures are all checked by historians. Working with generative AI is actually an extremely hands-on process. It still struggles with precise shot duration, complex movements, character continuity and continuity between shots. We constantly have to work around these limitations through directing and editing – changing an angle, breaking an action into several shots, moving from a close-up to a wide shot. Sometimes, a technical limitation actually leads us to find a stronger visual solution.

	Do you think AI is the future of how documentaries will be created?

	Contant: There will always be many different forms of documentary, just as fiction ranges from intimate films to major blockbusters. AI will not replace a director’s vision, investigative work or the filming of reality. But for the first time, documentaries have visual tools that can allow them to compete with fiction in terms of immersion and spectacle. Until now, CGI reenactments were often constrained by budgets far below those of cinema or video games. AI is radically changing that. I don’t think it will become the norm across every documentary genre. Social-issue documentaries, archive-based films and wildlife films operate according to very different principles. But for ambitious historical, scientific and factual storytelling, it opens up an extraordinary new creative territory.
	

	What are some of the historical facts about the Venationes that most surprised you?

	Contant: One of the first things I discovered was that the men who fought animals were not gladiators. There was another category of fighters: the Venatores, hunters specially trained to capture wild animals and confront them in staged combats in the arena. Some became genuine stars and drew huge crowds.I was also surprised to learn that the Roman army was involved in capturing animals. Soldiers used their expertise in strategy, logistics and siege techniques not only for warfare, but also for this vast entertainment industry. 

	But what probably struck me most was discovering the ecological impact of this entertainment industry. By capturing and killing animals by the thousands over several centuries, Rome contributed to the extinction of certain species, including, for example, the North African elephant. It is one of the earliest known examples of a civilization putting such intense pressure on wildlife purely for the purpose of entertainment.

schema.headline: Balanga Secures First International Sales for History Doc ‘Beasts of the Colosseum,’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Amazon's Newest Fire Tablet Is Only $150, With 10,000 Units Sold In the Last Month Alone
description: Amazon has made a name for itself with its slate of Alexa-enabled devices, but the retail giant is also a leader when it comes to its lineup of tabl
body:
Amazon has made a name for itself with its slate of Alexa-enabled devices, but the retail giant is also a leader when it comes to its lineup of tablets. Whether for work or streaming, Amazon’s Fire Tablets offer up huge value, especially when compared to Apple’s iPad or the Samsung Galaxy Tab.

	Case in point: A new deal gets you the all-new Fire HD 10 Tablet on sale for just $154.99, less than half the price of the cheapest iPad on Amazon. This is a bestseller on Amazon too, with the site reporting more than 10,000 units sold in the last few weeks alone. Almost 80% of shoppers, meantime, give the tablet a full, five-star review.


		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										A DO-IT-ALL DEVICE						

					Amazon Fire HD 10 Tablet		

		
	

	The Fire Tablet features a 10.1-inch full HD display with millions of dazzling pixels that bring your content to life in full, vivid color. Amazon says the Fire HD 10 is almost 20% brighter than the Samsung Galaxy Tab A8 when comparing the two side by side.

	With up to 13 hours of battery life, meantime, the Amazon Fire Tablet beats the iPad by three extra hours, letting you spend more time connected to your device and less time waiting for it to charge.

	Features-wise, the HD 10 Tablet comes with 32GB of storage, a super fast octa-core processor (that offers “25% faster performance than the previous generation,” per Amazon) and 4GB of RAM for instant responsiveness and smooth loading of all your apps and content.

	The 5MP front-facing camera is great for taking calls, while the 5MP rear-facing cameras can be used for snapping photos or shooting video in stunning 1080p HD quality. The tablet is great for streaming too, with Dolby Atmos sound and a large, crisp display.


	The Fire HD 10 Tablet is one of most durable tablets on the market, which makes it great for travel or commuting. Amazon says the Fire HD 10 was almost three times as durable as the Samsung Galaxy Tab A8 when measured in “tumble testing.” The Fire Tablet screen, meantime, is reinforced with a scratch-resistant aluminosilicate glass.

	The Fire Tablet can be used as an e-reader or as a digital notebook with the Amazon Stylus Pen (sold separately). Amazon says the tablet has been refined with more than 4,000 levels of “pressure sensitivity,” allowing it to better respond to your writing and sketching. We personally use a Fire Tablet to take notes during our weekly pitch meetings, share ideas (via Microsoft OneNote) and to keep track of assignments.

	The Amazon deal gets you a brand new Fire HD 10 Tablet for its cheapest price this year. You can save an additional 20% off if you trade-in an old device. See full details here.

title: Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Dang!’ Is an Enjoyably Chaotic Sibling Hangout: TV Review
description: The basic premise of the Netflix animated comedy “Dang!” bears a passing resemblance to that of “Broad City”: two codependent millennial burnouts li
body:
The basic premise of the Netflix animated comedy “Dang!” bears a passing resemblance to that of “Broad City”: two codependent millennial burnouts living and (barely) working in New York City. The difference is that this pair, Andrew (series creator Andrew Law) and Eunice (Poppy Liu), are siblings; the show’s title is also their last name, minus the interrobang. And the duo’s domestic bliss is interrupted by the arrival of a third party — their older sister Ruthie (Stephanie Hsu), an uptight lawyer whose midlife crisis brings her down to her brother and sister’s level.
	

	Then again, the “Broad City” parallels aren’t a complete coincidence. Law and Liu both previously worked on “Hacks,” whose three co-creators all cut their teeth on Ilana Glazer and Abbi Jacobson’s beloved stoner comedy. (Michael Schur, an executive producer on “Hacks,” serves in the same capacity on “Dang!”.) All three shows feature protagonists emblematic of downwardly mobile generational malaise, but any broader commentary takes a back seat to human relationships and, of course, jokes. Such is the case with “Dang!,” where the lived-in dynamic among the trio leads to a distinct take on the comforting familiarity of a family sitcom.


	Before Ruthie shows up, the younger Dangs are at peace with their own mediocrity. Eunice crushes bread with her feet for pay pigs on OnlyFans; when Andrew gets fired from the startup he co-founded for running an anonymous gossip account from his IBS-induced bathroom breaks, he’s happy to rejoin the company in a vanity job designing merch. Ruthie thinks she’s better than they are, and treasures their immigrant parents’ approval, but also envies the closeness that’s left her feeling excluded. (When Eunice argues that Ruthie shares her own secret language with their mom and dad, the attorney points out that she just speaks Mandarin because she paid attention in Chinese school.) This status quo starts to change when Ruthie gets pregnant via extramarital affair and moves to New York to figure out her life. “You’re one of us now, you stupid pregnant bitch!” Eunice squeals, her eyes going sparkly and anime-wide.
	

	For the middle stretch of its eight-episode season, “Dang!” puts Ruthie’s ticking time bomb of a secret (from her parents, at least) on hold to spend time on Andrew and Eunice’s aimless escapades. By the finale, Ruthie isn’t even showing yet, but we’ve watched Eunice try an experimental diet drug for her Goop-like unpaid internship and Andrew attempt to mentor a baby gay he knows from church youth group. (The fake praise song “Come Inside of Me” is pretty catchy!) Each Dang’s personality is clearly conceived and communicated through evocative detail: Ruthie’s preferred children’s book is “B Is for Border Security: How to Raise a Political Centrist”; Andrew is so people-pleasing he can barely decide on a bodega order; Eunice has a sixth sense that tells her when the uncensored video of Lenny Kravitz ripping his pants is back on YouTube. Law is playing the not-so-straight man amid the chaos, but both Liu and Hsu give vivid voice performances from opposite ends of the slacker-to-Type-A spectrum — Liu’s delivery laconic and always sounding a little stoned, Hsu’s sharp and aggressive.

	Many new comedies these days suffer from a compressed run that offers little room to riff and experiment. By keeping a tight focus on its nuclear unit, “Dang!” avoids this issue with a compact concept that never feels too big for its vessel. Besides, the backdrop against which Andrew, Eunice and Ruthie conduct their misadventures is the stuff of countless shows before it; beyond just “Broad City,” there’s “Sex and the City,” “Girls” and many more that obviate the need for exposition. Animation helps “Dang!” add some pizzazz to otherwise ordinary conflicts like Eunice puzzling out whether a guy she likes has an Asian fetish; instead of talking it out over brunch á la Carrie Bradshaw, she convenes a panel of celebrity cameos like Chloe Kim and Padma Lakshmi. Yet it’s the Dangs themselves, each dysfunctional in their own special way, who serve as the real draw.

	All eight episodes of “Dang!” are now streaming on Netflix.

schema.headline: Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Dang!’ Is an Enjoyably Chaotic Sibling Hangout: TV Review

title: Venice Horizons Winner Anuparna Roy Returns to Lido With Mumbai Story of Migrants, Desire and Belonging ‘Lovers in the Blue Night’
description:

body:
Indian filmmaker Anuparna Roy has been carrying Ameena’s story since childhood. 

	Ameena was a bonded laborer in Roy’s hometown, and something she once said about her marriage stayed with the director long after she grew up and moved away. That memory became the seed for “Lovers in the Blue Night,” which premieres in the Horizons competition at the Venice Film Festival a year after Roy’s debut feature, “Songs of Forgotten Trees,” made her the first Indian filmmaker to win the section’s best director prize. 
	

	International sales on the new film are being handled by Parallax.


	Roy says “Songs of Forgotten Trees” was a personal story made under difficult funding conditions, built around two women who barely leave a single house. “Lovers in the Blue Night” widens that frame to four migrants moving through Mumbai; she also describes the production itself as far more professional this time, with deadlines and limitations she is still learning to work inside.

	Asked whether she expected the new film to move into Venice’s main competition rather in Horizons, Roy says she dreamed of it rather than expected it, and that landing in the section again is no disappointment. She still considers herself a new director learning her craft alongside filmmakers she admires.

	Ameena’s arc did not stay fixed to the facts that Roy remembered. She says her early instinct was rebellious, imagining the character finding real love and leaving her marriage behind. But that path stopped looking like simple freedom as the script developed. “That is also another loop — another loop of patriarchy,” Roy says, describing what looks from the outside like an escape into a happy ending.
	

	That refusal to let escape read as simple freedom extends to how Roy treats her characters’ circumstances more broadly. She wanted the migrants’ hardship to shape them without defining them entirely, resisting the idea that displacement should crowd out their ordinary desires for intimacy, jealousy or tenderness. Karim, a closeted gay man married to Ameena, and his lover Sukka, a man trying to break free of caste, sit at the center of that approach. Roy says she wanted a neutral, empathetic language for both men rather than exaggerating poverty or turning their struggle into ideology.

	Roy frames love itself as a form of resistance for characters, who are punished for wanting things. “When you are lonely or displaced, even a small gesture of intimacy can begin to feel enormous,” she says, describing what she calls the illusion of love: a space where affection, longing, isolation, need and fantasy start to blur together, so that people fall for the possibility of a person as much as the person themselves.

	One choice stands out. Karim produces rat poison and kills rats in wealthy Mumbai housing societies, a job Roy based on someone she saw doing the same work in the city’s Andheri East suburb. She calls the image of him coming home from that job to kiss another man “no less than revolutionary,” and says placing the two things side by side felt deeply political to her.

	Displacement links this film to Roy’s debut. Both stories draw on floods Roy experienced growing up in a coastal region near the Bangladesh border, close to the Bay of Bengal, and both send their characters into exile from a destroyed home. Where her first film explored two women, this one turns to two men and the duality of bisexuality.

	Upcoming stories include “In the Shadow in the Light,” a romantic feature about a dysfunctional marriage modeled partly on her parents, and an untitled project about a woman’s sexual transit.

schema.headline: Venice Horizons Winner Anuparna Roy Returns to Lido With Mumbai Story of Migrants, Desire and Belonging ‘Lovers in the Blue Night’

title: Inside the Restoration of Indian Cult Classic ‘English, August,’ Heading to Venice as Relevant as Ever (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Dev Benegal‘s “English, August” almost didn’t survive to be restored. Its original camera negative had melted. The dupe was gone too. All that was l
body:
Dev Benegal‘s “English, August” almost didn’t survive to be restored. Its original camera negative had melted. The dupe was gone too. All that was left were two surviving 35mm prints – and, it turned out, a box of DAT tapes nobody expected to matter three decades later.

	“It’s really sad that when I saw the original camera negative, it had melted. It was in terrible condition,” says Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founder of the Film Heritage Foundation (FHF), the organization that took on the restoration. FHF was left to rebuild the film from whatever prints remained.
	

	What remained were two 35mm release prints: one Benegal had personally kept and donated to FHF, the other preserved by the NFDC-National Film Archive of India, the government body that houses India’s official film archive. “There was no other material, so we had to look at both these materials, do the comparison and use these particular prints,” Dungarpur says. Both prints, he says, were in decent condition – a stroke of luck given how little else of the film had survived.


	Released in 1994, “English, August” follows Agastya Sen, a young, Westernized trainee nicknamed “August,” sent to a remote provincial town for a year of civil-service training in India’s elite administrative cadre. Adrift among Bob Dylan records, Marcus Aurelius and a bureaucracy he can barely stomach, Agastya finds himself a stranger in a country that is technically his own. The film is adapted from Upamanyu Chatterjee’s 1988 novel of the same name, a book that became a defining portrait of a certain post-colonial, urban Indian generation.
	

	Benegal says the screenplay only became the film in the editing room. “This is a film which was truly written on the editing table. I am a firm believer that’s where movies are actually written,” he says. “While we were editing, Upamanyu asked me, ‘Why did we even write a screenplay? We are writing the film right here.'”

	The soundtrack turned out to be the restoration’s unlikely triumph. Benegal recalls the constraints under which the film was originally mixed. “Vikram Joglekar had recorded the sound in digital. Ignoring industry advice not to do that!” he says. “In 1994 we did not have the money to create a stereo mix. Those were days of the License Raj, where we had to secure special permission to import six reels of Kodak Optical Sound Negative. Even after that we only had outdated equipment to make a flat mono mix.” What survived instead was a set of DAT tapes Benegal had quietly kept for thirty years. “Back in 1994, DATs were the cutting-edge digital recording medium, and I kept them in my personal archive purely out of my obsession with audio – never imagining they would save the film three decades later when the original 35mm sound negatives vanished,” he says. “Going back to those tapes with Vikram Joglekar was like opening a time capsule.” Dungarpur confirms the tapes gave FHF something restorers rarely get. “We went back to the studio, and Vikram Joglekar, who was the sound recordist, brought back Satish P.M., the sound engineer, to work on restoring these tracks,” he says. “We had the unmixes, so it was great.”

	Color grading brought its own rhythm to the process. Dungarpur says the palette was set by cinematographer Anoop Jotwani, who tested a single reel before the rest of the film followed his lead, with Benegal weighing in throughout from New York as the restoration work itself took place at L’Immagine Ritrovata, the film lab in Bologna, Italy. “You had Dev Benegal working almost daily on it. He did the English subtitles. We were talking daily about the look of the film, the way it was restored in Bologna, the grains and the color tone,” Dungarpur says. “There was a constant flow between Bologna and Dev Benegal, who was sitting in New York. He actually booked a suite to look at the grading, to look at the colors, to hear the sound.” Rahul Bose, who made his feature debut as the film’s lead, also came in to see part of the process, Dungarpur says.
	

	Benegal is unequivocal about why Bose was right for that role. “Rahul Bose understood that Agastya wasn’t someone the audience needed to like; he needed to be truthful,” Benegal says. “He wasn’t trying to perform alienation – he simply inhabited the character with remarkable honesty. He also had the confidence to do very little. That’s much harder than it sounds.”

	Not everything about the soundtrack could be fully reconstructed. Benegal says the production had gone to unusual lengths at the time to license its music. “Back in the day the producing team worked tirelessly to license and pay for music rights – something virtually unheard of then in India,” he says. One piece of paperwork never made it. “The paperwork documenting the Miles Davis’ “‘Round Midnight” clearance was lost in a torrential monsoon flood,” he says. The gap has created its own folklore among fans, he adds: “Some people have made a mix tape in their minds, from the box of tapes Agastya carried with him to Madna. Those tracks were never actually part of the original theatrical mix. Memory has a curious way of creating its own version of a film.”

	For Dungarpur, the restoration answered a demand that had been building for years. “There was a great demand by people who wanted, were looking for, something to watch it back on the big screen and to see a restoration of this,” he says of “English, August.” “There are many people coming from around the world” eager to see the film again, he adds, calling it one of the independently produced films FHF exists to bring back “into a different time” for new audiences – including at Venice where the restoration premieres. It’s also FHF’s third consecutive year premiering a restoration at the festival, following Girish Kasaravalli’s “Ghatashraddha” in 2024 and Bimal Roy’s “Do Bigha Zamin” in 2025. 

	Watching “English, August” again more than 32 years after making it, Benegal finds the film’s portrait of isolation has only sharpened. “What feels familiar is the uncertainty,” he says. “India in the early 1990s was beginning to open up economically and culturally, but the old structures still shaped everyday life. There was a generation caught between inherited institutions and emerging freedoms. That sense of being in transition still resonates.” What has changed entirely, he says, is the texture of being alone. “The film unfolds in an India before mobile phones, social media and constant connectivity. Agastya is left alone with his thoughts… In 1994, if you were exiled to a small district town, you were genuinely off the grid. Agastya’s isolation was spatial and physical; today, isolation is algorithmic.”
	

	Benegal argues the character’s alienation was never really about the West. “Agastya isn’t alienated because he listens to rock and jazz or reads Marcus Aurelius. He’s alienated because he’s searching for authenticity in a role that feels imposed upon him. That’s a condition that transcends both geography and time,” he says. He sees that same restlessness in a different uniform today: “The modern Agastyas aren’t just urban civil servants reading Marcus Aurelius in small towns – they are scrolling through curated, globalized lives on their phones from anywhere. The absurdity hasn’t disappeared; it’s just been upgraded to high-speed internet.”

	The film’s satire of Indian bureaucracy has aged in a similar direction, according to Benegal. “Three decades later, the language of bureaucracy may have been digitized, but the core absurdities – the performance of power and the gap between official intent and ground reality – remain unchanged,” he says. “If anything, the satire feels almost prescient today.”

	Benegal is candid that the film could not be made the same way now. “‘English, August’ succeeded precisely because it fit into zero existing boxes – it rejected that one prescribed way of making films,” he says. The five languages spoken across the film famously baffled censors at the time: “English, August has five languages, and that stumped the Indian censors who insisted, ‘a film can only have one language.'” Distribution came down to one gamble. “I have to give a huge shout out to Sunder Kimat Rai, who was country head of 20th Century Fox at that time, who took the gamble to distribute the film. He said, ‘the demographics match.’ I had no idea what ‘demographics’ even meant,” Benegal says. He doubts that kind of bet would be made today. “While we have streaming platforms and festival infrastructure, we also have hyper-calculated algorithms. Everything gets filtered through target demographics, pitch decks, and comparative commercial comps. The tools to shoot and edit are democratized, but the willingness of financiers and distributors to take a gamble on pure, unclassifiable tone is far rarer.”

	Asked what a 20-year-old watching the film today might see that 1994 audiences couldn’t, Benegal points to something less generational than it first appears. “I hope they watch it as a portrait of someone asking timeless questions: Who am I? What kind of life do I want? What happens when the expectations of society don’t align with your inner life?” he says. “A young audience today may recognise mental and emotional states that weren’t discussed as openly in 1994. Agastya’s uncertainty may feel less like aimlessness and more like an honest search for meaning.”
	

	Benegal is already looking past the restoration to his next project. “I’m working on ‘A Love Supreme’ a contemporary re-imagining of the epic Shakuntala – a story of a resilient, enigmatic woman whose path defies societal norms to become an autonomous woman,” he says. “But, the impulse remains the same as it was in 1994 – finding the humor, absurdity, and humanity in spaces where people feel out of place.”

schema.headline: Inside the Restoration of Indian Cult Classic ‘English, August,’ Heading to Venice as Relevant as Ever (EXCLUSIVE)

title: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Crosses $300 Million
description: Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” retained the top spot at the mainland China box office for the fourth consecut
body:
Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” retained the top spot at the mainland China box office for the fourth consecutive weekend, grossing RMB82.6 million ($12.1 million) over the Sept. 4–6 frame, according to data from Artisan Gateway. 

	The blockbuster hit has now crossed a major milestone, lifting its cumulative total to $305.6 million since its nationwide launch on Aug. 11. Directed by Wen Muye (“Dying to Survive”) from a script co-written with Lang Qunli and Wei Zhong, the film stars Shen Teng as a debt-ridden Chinese chef in the Middle East who, alongside his floor manager (Jiang Qiming), transforms his eatery into a vital safe haven for civilians and orphans amidst erupting regional conflict. The cast also features Aarif Rahman and Omar Sherif.
	

	Pearl River Film Group’s crime thriller “V” maintained second place, bringing in $7.9 million in its third weekend for a cumulative total of $75.4 million. Directed by Han Yan (“Love Never Ends”), the film stars Tony Ka Fai Leung, Zhu Yilong, Tan Jianci, and Kara Wai in a cautionary tale charting an ambitious figure’s rise to prominence and the dangerous consequences that accompany his ambition.


	Universal’s “The Odyssey” took third position in its fourth frame, collecting $5.5 million. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan, the Imax-shot adaptation of Homer’s ancient Greek epic has amassed a cumulative gross of $97.4 million. 

	Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy feature “All Wishes Come True!” continued its summer endurance run in fourth place, adding $4.8 million in its eighth weekend of release. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the mythological comedy has accumulated a stellar $277.5 million since opening on July 18.
	

	Capstone Pictures’ survival thriller “Fall 2: Deadpoint” debuted in fifth position, generating $3 million over its opening weekend and $3.2 million including early screenings since launching Sept. 4. 

	Mainland China’s overall weekend grosses reached $41.9 million, while the 2026 year-to-date revenue stands at $4.21 billion, down 27.8% from the same period in 2025.

schema.headline: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Crosses $300 Million

title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Overwhelms ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ as Admissions Top 10 Million
description:
“The Odyssey” held onto its commanding lead at the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sep. 4–6. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the trac
body:
“The Odyssey” held onto its commanding lead at the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sep. 4–6. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Christopher Nolan-directed tentpole generated $5.9 million from 698,384 admissions over the three-day frame across 1,858 screens, capturing 60.92% of the total weekend market. With its fifth consecutive weekend victory, the blockbuster officially crossed the milestone of ten million admissions, pushing its cumulative haul to $83.2 million from 10,027,970 total viewers since its Aug. 5 debut.
	

	Superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” retained second place in its sixth outing, generating $942,178 from 146,674 admissions across 725 screens. It accounted for 9.6% of the weekend market, lifting its cumulative South Korean gross to $67.9 million from 8,792,026 total ticket buyers.


	Curry Barker’s “Obsession” debuted in third place, pulling in $1.1 million from 138,447 admissions over the three-day frame across 717 screens. Including mid-week business since its Sep. 2 opening, the sleeper horror entry has accumulated $1.4 million from 185,100 total viewers.

	Local family road-trip drama “The Journey to Gyeongju” took fourth place in its sophomore weekend, generating $359,527 from 49,417 admissions. Directed by Kim Mi-jo and starring Lee Jung-eun, Gong Hyo-jin, Park So-dam, Lee Yeon, and Byun Yo-han, the revenge-tinged family narrative moved its cumulative total to $2.1 million from 297,594 admissions.

	The local family crime-drama “Portrait of a Family” opened in fifth place, earning $286,526 from 40,835 admissions over the weekend. Directed by Lee Ji-won and starring Ryu Seung-ryong and Ha Ji-won, the film centers on a former superstar baseball player and a top actress whose glamorous lives unravel when a mysterious young girl appears, dragging them into a desperate struggle seven years later. Since its Sep. 2 launch, the film has collected $484,757 from 71,392 admissions.
	

	“Power Ballad” debuted in sixth place, collecting $251,801 from 34,382 admissions across 591 screens. Since its Sep. 2 premiere, the feature has grossed $399,799 from 55,931 admissions.

	Animated fantasy sequel “Teenieping: Legend of the Whale Heartstone” was in seventh place, adding $120,759 from 16,715 admissions. Directed by Kim Soo-hoon, the family film has pushed its cumulative gross to $6 million from 858,707 admissions since its Aug. 5 rollout.

	The upcoming local comedy-drama “The Intern” landed in eighth place ahead of its official wide release, bringing in $91,227 from 11,989 admissions across early preview screenings. Directed by Kim Do-young, the local remake of Nancy Meyers’ 2015 Hollywood film follows a seasoned senior citizen who enters the workforce anew as a senior intern at an energetic fashion startup.

	Toho’s anime mystery “Detective Conan the Movie: Fallen Angel of the Highway” placed ninth, collecting $60,695 from 7,953 admissions over the frame. Directed by Takahiro Hasui, the franchise instalment has reached a cumulative total of $3.1 million from 420,629 viewers.

	Rounding out the top 10 was “The End of Oak Street,” which took $55,192 from 7,511 admissions over its second frame, pushing its South Korean cume to $967,625 from 130,502 admissions.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $9.8 million, down from last week’s $13.5 million, continuing the post-summer box office slowdown.

title: Lumiere Declaration Sets 15 Principles for Global Film Governance, Calling Audience Attention ‘a Trust to Be Honored, Not a Resource to Be Captured’
description: Representatives of countries, international organizations, film, television and gaming industry leaders, creators, festivals and cultural institutio
body:
Representatives of countries, international organizations, film, television and gaming industry leaders, creators, festivals and cultural institutions from across the world adopted the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image on Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence.

	Jointly presented by France and the Republic of Korea and convened under the co-chairship of their respective presidents, the declaration sets out 15 principles and remains open for further signatures. “We lay here the foundations of a multilateralism of the moving image,” it states – a framework adopted 200 years after the first photograph and 130 years after the Lumière brothers’ first public screening of the Cinématographe, and one the declaration describes as the beginning of something new: “the moving image now has the beginnings of a global governance – a multilateralism meant to grow, through new initiatives, new partners and future gatherings.”
	

	What the declaration argues, at its core, is that moving images exist for more than the capture of attention. They are, it states, “a common good: a vehicle for emotion, memory and knowledge, for individual emancipation and collective transformation.” Ambitious, intentional works “remain irreplaceable,” and “the future of our industries will be defined by the works we choose to create and support.” 


	The sharpest line in the document draws a direct contrast with algorithmic platforms: “The attention of an audience is not a resource to be captured, but a trust to be honored.” That conviction runs through several further principles — on who makes stories (“the richness of the stories we tell depends on the diversity of those who create them”), on the conditions under which they are made (“freedom of creation is a condition of the vitality and diversity of the moving image”), and on those who face “political, economic or social pressures that threaten their ability to create and to be heard,” for whom the declaration backs international networks of solidarity. An industry that excludes women or operates in unsafe conditions, it states, must become “exemplary in the exercise” of its power to shape representations.
	

	On economics, the declaration is equally explicit. “A powerful engine of economic growth” is how it describes the audiovisual industry – one that “drives investment across a broad range of businesses, creates jobs, cultivates a highly skilled workforce, fosters innovation.” Distributors and others who profit from exploiting works carry “both a responsibility and a direct interest in the next generation of creation,” it states, calling for public support to enable early-stage risk-taking and for conditions that allow creators to develop their work over time. “International co-production diversifies risk, enriches works and binds our ecosystems together,” it adds, with a commitment to deepen cooperation between established and emerging markets “so that the diversity of the world’s stories finds its way onto the world’s screens.” The commercial case for breadth of output is put plainly: “The diversity of works, across budgets, languages, genres, formats and geographies, is not a constraint on competitiveness; it is its foundation.”

	Three of the 15 principles address technology. “Artificial intelligence can strengthen creativity, innovation and the circulation of works – provided it becomes a driver of creation,” the declaration states, adding that “human creation should always remain at the heart and foundation of works.” On discoverability, it flags a risk no multilateral document has previously named – the rise of agentic AI – warning of “the possible advent of a world in which access to works would increasingly be mediated by automated agents.” On piracy: “When creation is not rewarded, it cannot be renewed.”

	The remaining principles address the physical and cultural infrastructure the industry depends on. “Diversity needs cinemas in order to thrive; cinemas need diversity in order to fulfill their cultural, economic and social role,” the declaration states on theatrical exhibition. On heritage, it warns of “the critical period for the conservation of physical archives, whose elements degrade inexorably over time,” calling for investment and solidarity so that “every country can pass its memory on, alive and visible, to future generations.” On education: “Just as previous centuries pursued universal literacy in the written word, the age of images demands an equally ambitious commitment to image literacy,” with cinema identified as “one of the last places where individual screens are switched off and where we learn, again, to watch together.” A final principle commits signatories to developing “best practices, flexible standards, and practical tools for the design and implementation of sustainable production, distribution and exhibition.”
	

	The signatories committed to remain collectively engaged and to review progress together.

title: About Premium Content Inks International Deals for Mystery and Romance Series, Counterfeit Art Doc (EXCLUSIVE)
description: APC Studios’ boutique distributor About Premium Content (APC) has signed a number of key international broadcast deals ahead of this year’s Unifranc
body:
APC Studios’ boutique distributor About Premium Content (APC) has signed a number of key international broadcast deals ahead of this year’s Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre on French-language scripted and unscripted series “Blue Gold,” “Seasons” and “An Artful Imbrolio.”

	The eight-part crime drama and family saga “Blue Gold” has been licensed to Walter Presents for the U.K. and Ireland, RTP in Portugal and Blue Play in Switzerland, joining U.S. streamer MHz Choice.
	

	Produced by Authentic Prod (“Sam,” “Montmartre”) for France Télévisions the series is written by Marie-Anne Le Pezennec (“Dolmen”) and Ludovix Lacroix and directed by Hippolyte Dard.




	

					Barbara Probst stars in ‘Blue Gold’
									Courtesy of About Premium Content
	



	Set in the 1980s in Provence, “Blue Gold” chronicles the saga of three women from three generations, Marie, Alice and Flore, and one decades-old buried secret. When a body is found and murders start piling up, Flore will have to solve the family puzzle by revealing the truth. Barbara Probst, Sylvie Granotier and Déborah Krey star. 

	The four-part “Seasons,” a French-language drama series produced by Windy Production for Arte, has been picked up by RTP in Portugal and RTBF Auvio for French-speaking Belgium. It previously sold to Radio Canada’s Ici Tou.TV Extra for French-speaking Canada.



	

					‘Seasons’
									Courtesy of About Premium Content
	



	Beginning in August 1991 at the seaside resort of Les-Sables-d’Olonne, it follows Camille, 15, as she first meets the two best friends Martin and Alexandre on the beach and crashes into their lives like a comet. Perpetually torn between the two men, Camille will live a crazy love story with them over more than 30 years.
	

	Nicolas Maury (“Call My Agent”) directed, co-wrote and stars in the show, co-written by Hélène Duchateau (“The Forest,” “Unfaithful,” “The Eclipse”). The series’ stellar cast includes Stéphane Caillard (“Flo,” “Marseille”), Lucas Bravo (“Emily in Paris,” “Ticket to Paradise”), Abraham Wapler (“Andor,” “Colours of Time”), Géraldine Pailhas, Martine Chevallie and Marysole Fertard.

	APC Stories’ three-part art investigation documentary “An Artful Imbroglio” went to Filmin in Spain and RTP in Portugal. Produced for Arte, the unscripted series, which is set in Paris, Rome, London and New York, sheds light on one of the art world’s greatest mysteries.

	In the spring of 2014, a mysterious, anonymous letter triggered one of the biggest scandals in the art world: the alleged trafficking of fake old master paintings on an unprecedented scale. At the heart of this imbroglio unfolds a gallery of colorful characters, all revolving around an ultra-charismatic art dealer.

title: Prada Foundation Film Fund Chief Paolo Moretti on First-Year Journey That Helped  Spawn Rubaiyat Hossain’s Venice Horizons Entry ‘The Difficult Bride’
description: Last year at the Venice Film Festival, Italy’s Fondazione Prada officially launched its film fund, aimed at sustaining independent cinema from aroun
body:
Last year at the Venice Film Festival, Italy’s Fondazione Prada officially launched its film fund, aimed at sustaining independent cinema from around the world without any restrictions on theme, genre or language. This year, it‘s back on the Lido with tangible proof that the initiative has borne fruit.

	The fund’s first edition is among backers of Bangladeshi director Rubaiyat Hossain’s “The Difficult Bride,” which is competing in the fest’s Horizons section. Meanwhile, winners of its second round of financing will be announced in February.
	

	Variety talked to Paolo Moretti, the former Cannes Directors’ Fortnight chief, who is managing the fund in collaboration with film programmer Rebecca De Pas, about its first-year journey.

	
		How has the last year unfolded for the fund?	

	We have been pleasantly surprised. In a very short time, we’ve managed to establish a real line of communication with a large segment of the industry. We had a truly massive number of projects applying, roughly 1,200.  It usually takes time for new initiatives like this to gain a foothold, but the interest in our proposed format — which is relatively unique in the world of film funding — was immediate. We then had to deal with this huge volume of projects. From one perspective this was thrilling, as it gave us a vivid picture of the vitality of contemporary cinema and showed us just how many people still believe in it. We are interested in cinema that breaks new ground. We subsequently adapted our structure — specifically the number of readers and collaborators — to handle this volume, because we wanted to treat every single project submitted to us with the seriousness and attention it deserved.
	
	
		What tweaks did you make?	

	When we announced the 14 selected projects in Berlin, there were only supposed to be 12. We managed to support two additional ones because in the end we saw that, despite the [limited] overall amount [of resources] we have available for the fund, not everyone had requested the maximum amount, so this allowed us to adjust the support in quantitative terms. Then we started following the progress of the projects. From February onwards, we started getting updates and news, including the wonderful news of Rubaiyat Hossain’s film being selected for Venice. At the same time, we were trying to think about how to evolve the system and improve it. One of the first ideas that came to us was to separate the submission of projects that are in production phase — which I would say are the vast majority — from those in development and post-production to try to balance out these three segments.
	
		What is the criteria in terms of the budgets of the films you are supporting?	

	There is no written criteria because we want to give ourselves the possibility of making exceptions if we fall in love with a project, so there’s no budget limit. However, the discussions we had, and the final selection process, tell us this: We ended up choosing projects that cost between a few hundred thousand euros up to five million. In short, this is the range. And, among other things, this is the budget range at which most experimental arthouse cinema is produced, and that is precisely what we want to support. But that doesn’t mean that if we come across a project that might be a little more expensive, but that resonates very, very pertinently with the spirit of the fund, we won’t support it.
	
		Regarding the overall budget, what is the prospect that the €1.5 million ($1.6 million) pot could increase?	

	For now, that is the available budget. Clearly the number of projects we’ve received tells us that there is a need for this support. So I’d say we can’t rule out an increase. Personally, I can only hope so. But I think the foundation is already doing something truly unique and extremely useful and generous.

Steve-O

                              September 8, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Steve-O just built an Olympic-length pool in his Tennessee backyard ... and naturally, he cemented a "Jackass" butt plug into it.
      
    
            The 82-foot heated lap pool was built by Pool and Spa Depot, and Steve-O tells TMZ it's part of his latest health and wellness push. He claims his biometrics now show he's 7,800% more fit than he was in February ... and he swam over 3 miles in the pool's first two days.
      
    
            Steve-O also buried a few keepsakes in the concrete -- his handprints, signature, a 1-pound anvil and his medallion marking 18 years of sobriety.
      

            But the wildest addition came courtesy of Johnny Knoxville.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve-O says Knoxville had butt plugs made for the "Jackass" cast featuring director Jeff Tremaine's head ... and he wanted one cemented into the pool to honor the franchise and the friendships it gave him.
      
    
            Problem was, Steve-O had lost his ... so he hit the "Jackass" group chat asking someone to overnight one before the concrete was poured.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sure enough, two showed up in the mail just in time to make the concrete pour.
      
    
            Steve-O says the new pool will help him train year-round ... and next month he's planning to run two triathlons in one week, including his first Olympic-distance race.

title: Fake Pro Basketball Player Accused of Stealing $90K BMW From Valet
description:
Fake Pro Basketball Player
                          Allegedly Stole $90K BMW From Valet
body:
Fake Pro Basketball Player
                          Allegedly Stole $90K BMW From Valet
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A man accused of posing as a pro basketball player apparently took his fake baller act straight to the valet stand ... where cops say he drove off in a $90,000 BMW that wasn't his.
      
    
            Savannah, Georgia police say the suspect walked into the Hyatt Regency Savannah around 12:30 AM on Aug. 14, grabbed some belongings from a white Audi, then handed valet workers a ticket for a gray 2026 BMW X5.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to investigators, he told employees he was a professional basketball player with several cars at the hotel ... and apparently sold the story well enough to get the keys and peel out in the BMW.
      

            Problem is ... police say the SUV actually belonged to a dealership and was being used as a loaner by a hotel guest. The dealership later tracked it all the way to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            And the alleged car-hopping didn't stop there -- investigators later learned the white 2025 Audi A5 he'd been seen using was itself reported stolen the day before. Cops found it unlocked in the hotel's parking garage later that morning.
      
    
            Police also believe the same guy may be tied to another valet theft at a Savannah hotel earlier in August ... when a guest's Toyota C-HR disappeared after someone allegedly used her retrieval code given to her from the valet service hours before she requested the car.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Savannah police have released surveillance images of the suspect, described as a man in his 20s or 30s, as they try to identify him.
      
    
            Move over, Daejon Love ...

title: 'South Park' Mocks Donald Trump After Winning Emmy
description:
'South Park' to Trump
                          Here's the Emmy You Never Won!!!
body:
'South Park' to Trump
                          Here's the Emmy You Never Won!!!
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "South Park" just added another Emmy to its trophy case ... and immediately handed President Trump the punchline.
      
    
            The Comedy Central series won Outstanding Animated Program Sunday for "Sermon On The 'Mount," an episode that heavily satirized Trump and even depicted him in bed with Satan.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            After the win, the show's social media account posted an image of its animated Trump clutching the trophy with the message, "You finally got your Emmy."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The joke goes back to Trump's history with the awards -- "The Apprentice" scored Emmy nominations in 2004 and 2005 but never took home the trophy, something Trump has publicly complained about over the years.
      
    
            Sunday's victory marked "South Park's" fifth Emmy in the animated program category.
      
    
            So, after decades of waiting, Trump finally got an Emmy ... he just had to move to South Park to get it.
